title: The Lord Has Become Like an Enemy
summary: The second poem describes the destruction of Jerusalem as the work of God's own anger: he has cut down Israel's strength, rejected his altar, torn down the walls, and silenced king, priest, and prophet. The poet breaks down over children fainting from hunger in the streets, blames the false prophets, and urges the city to pour out her heart to the Lord. Zion's prayer at the end asks whether anyone has ever been treated like this.
story: Chapter 1 dwelt on Jerusalem's loneliness and shame. Chapter 2 turns to the hardest question in the book: who did this? The answer is not only Babylon. Again and again the poem says He: the Lord has swallowed, demolished, cut off, burned. This is the fulfillment of what the covenant warned and what the prophets announced. The LORD has done what He planned (verse 17). The poem does not pretend that knowing this makes the suffering easier. Instead it moves from description to tears, and from tears to prayer, showing how a people can bring even God's judgment back to God.
historical:
The chapter draws on the events of 587 or 586 BC. The Babylonian army besieged Jerusalem for about eighteen months; food ran out (Jeremiah 52:6); the walls were breached; and the city, temple, and palaces were burned. Verse 9 notes that the king and princes are exiled among the nations: Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon, and his officials were executed or deported (Jeremiah 52:10-11, 24-27). The priests and prophets killed in the sanctuary (verse 20) reflect the slaughter when the city fell (2 Chronicles 36:17).

The poem's blame of the prophets (verse 14) fits what Jeremiah reports of the years before the fall. Prophets such as Hananiah had promised that Babylon's power would soon be broken and that the exiles would return within two years (Jeremiah 28:1-4). Others kept saying peace, peace, when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Their comforting visions kept the people from facing their guilt and turning back while there was still time.
cultural:
The temple was understood as the place where God's presence rested on earth. Verse 1 calls it his footstool, a term used elsewhere for the ark of the covenant and the temple (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7): God was pictured as enthroned in heaven with his feet resting in Jerusalem. The appointed feasts and Sabbaths (verse 6) were the rhythm of Israel's life with God; their end meant that the calendar of worship itself had stopped. The shout raised in the house of the LORD (verse 7) is the noise of enemy soldiers in the courts where festival crowds used to sing.

The elders who sit on the ground in silence with dust on their heads and sackcloth on their bodies (verse 10) are performing the standard rites of mourning in the ancient world. Sackcloth was a coarse cloth of goat hair; dust or ashes on the head signaled humiliation and grief. Siege warfare was the most feared kind of war in antiquity because famine inside the walls killed more people than the fighting, and those who suffered first were the weak. The horror of verse 20, mothers eating their children, is one of the curses of Deuteronomy 28:53-57 for covenant unfaithfulness, and it had happened before, during the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29).
literary: Like chapter 1, this poem is an alphabetic acrostic of twenty-two three-line stanzas, though here the Hebrew letters pe and ayin appear in reverse of their usual order, as they also do in chapters 3 and 4. It falls into three parts. Verses 1 to 10 describe God's anger, piling up verbs of destruction with God as their subject. Verses 11 to 19 shift to the poet's own voice: his eyes fail from weeping, he searches for a comparison that could console Zion and finds none, and he urges the city to cry out to God day and night. Verses 20 to 22 give Zion's reply, a prayer that is almost an accusation. The poem uses bold imagery (God bending his bow like an enemy, laying waste his tabernacle like a garden booth) and a shocking directness. The phrase the day of His anger frames the poem (verses 1 and 22).

outline.t: The Lord's anger: palaces, altar, walls, king, and prophets brought down
The poet's tears over the children and the false prophets
A call to cry out to the Lord
Zion's prayer: Whom have You ever treated like this

doctrines.note: The poem refuses to explain Jerusalem's fall as mere politics. God's anger is its cause, and his judgment fulfills what he warned “in days of old” (verse 17). Judgment is the dark side of God's holiness toward a covenant people who persistently rejected him.

The suffering of children and infants (verses 11, 12, 19, 20) is described without softening. Scripture does not hide the fact that judgment on a society falls on the innocent within it, and the poet's tears show that such suffering is rightly grieved rather than justified in the abstract.

“Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord” (verse 19). Even when God is experienced as the source of the pain, the poem sends the sufferer toward him, not away. Zion's prayer in verse 20 shows that honest protest is a form of prayer.
The false prophets' visions “were empty and deceptive” (verse 14), and now even true prophets find no vision (verse 9). A word that flatters instead of exposing sin leaves a people defenseless.

words.note: Aph, nose or face, and by extension anger, from the image of flaring nostrils. It appears six times in this chapter, framing it with the day of His anger. Hebrew speaks of God's anger in physical, burning terms, not to make him petty but to show that he is not indifferent to evil.

Bala, to swallow up. Used five times here: the Lord has swallowed Jacob's dwellings, Israel, her palaces; and the enemies boast that they have swallowed her. The image is of total destruction, as when the earth swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:32).

Chamal, to spare or have pity. The refrain that God acted without pity (verses 2, 17, and 21) is the heart of the city's anguish. Elsewhere the same verb describes compassion, as when Pharaoh's daughter pitied the infant Moses (Exodus 2:6). Its absence here is what makes the day so dark.

Chazon, vision, the revelation given to a prophet. Verse 9 laments that the prophets find no vision from the LORD; verse 14 says the visions that were given were false. Losing a true word from God is part of the judgment (compare Amos 8:11-12).

christ: This chapter does not predict Christ, and its connection to him runs through the theme of God's wrath. The poem describes what it is like when God's anger falls on his people, and the New Testament teaches that Jesus bore that wrath in their place. At the cross he entered the darkness this chapter describes: abandoned, mocked by passers-by who shook their heads (verse 15 has the same gesture; compare Mark 15:29), and crying out to God. Jesus also wept over Jerusalem and foretold that it would again be surrounded and torn down (Luke 19:41-44), which happened in AD 70. The link is one of pattern: the Son of God stood where Zion stood, so that those united to him need never hear God's final verdict as an enemy's.

hard.q: How can the Bible say that God acted like an enemy and killed without pity, even allowing children to starve?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest passages in Scripture, and it should be read slowly. First, the poet is not describing God's character in the abstract; he is describing how the disaster felt from inside it, and the Bible lets that experience stand in its own words. He says the Lord is like an enemy, a simile, not that he has become one in his nature. Second, the poem attributes the fall to covenant judgment that God had warned of for generations, not to caprice. Third, the book itself holds this beside the confession that the Lord does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men (3:33) and that his mercies never fail (3:22). Some interpreters stress God's sovereignty over the disaster; others stress that God let the consequences of the nation's choices and Babylon's cruelty run their course. Both agree that the suffering of children is a horror, not a lesson, and the poet weeps over it rather than excusing it. Readers carrying grief of their own, especially the loss of a child, will find here permission to protest before God. If that grief begins to feel unbearable, please speak with someone you trust or a counselor, and if you are thinking of ending your life, call or text 988 in the United States or contact a local crisis line.

questions: Why do you think the poet refuses to blame only Babylon for Jerusalem's fall? What is gained and what is risked by seeing God's hand in disaster?
The false prophets offered comforting visions that hid the people's guilt. Where are you tempted to prefer a comforting word to a true one?
The poet tells Zion to pour out her heart like water before the Lord. What keeps you from praying that honestly?
